topic: The Inscribed Square Problem: A Topological Journey
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with an interest in geometry

sections.title: The Hook: The Pirate's Square Treasure
sections.content: Introduce the central question: For any simple, closed loop (Jordan curve), can we always find four points on that loop that form the vertices of a perfect square? This is known as the Toeplitz Conjecture.
sections.example: An explorer finds a wobbly, irregular island coastline. He wants to place four observation towers at the corners of a perfect square along the shore. No matter how jagged the coast is, can he always do it?

sections.title: Prerequisite: Defining the 'Jordan Curve'
sections.content: Explain what a Jordan curve is: a non-self-intersecting continuous loop in a plane. Use visual animations to show the difference between a simple loop (like a rubber band) and a complex one (like a figure-eight, which is not a Jordan curve).
sections.example: Visualizing a 'wobbly circle' that can be stretched and pulled like dough, but never torn or crossed over itself.

sections.title: The Stepping Stone: The Inscribed Rectangle
sections.content: Before tackling the square, we look at the rectangle. This is a proven theorem. We introduce the concept of 'Pairs of Points'. Any two points on the curve define a potential side or diagonal.
sections.example: An ant and a beetle crawl along the loop. We track their positions and the distance between them to find symmetry.

sections.title: The Topological Trick: The Möbius Strip Mapping
sections.content: Introduce the brilliant proof for rectangles. We map every pair of points $(A, B)$ on the curve to a point in 3D space. The set of all unordered pairs of points on a circle topologically forms a Möbius Strip. We show how the 'boundary' of the curve maps to the edge of the strip.
sections.example: An animation showing a flat loop being transformed into a 3D Möbius strip. When this strip is dipped into a plane, the intersections represent the vertices of our rectangle.

sections.title: The Core Logic: Why One Surface Must Intersect Another
sections.content: Explain that because a Möbius strip has a boundary that maps to the curve itself, any surface spanning that boundary must intersect itself or a specific plane. This intersection point in the abstract 'space of pairs' corresponds to a set of points that form a rectangle in the real world.
sections.example: Imagine trying to flatten a crumpled piece of paper (the Möbius strip) onto a table. Because of its twist, it is forced to overlap itself; those overlaps are the secret locations of our rectangle corners.

sections.title: The Final Mystery: Square vs. Rectangle
sections.content: Discuss the current status of the problem. While rectangles are guaranteed for all Jordan curves, the 'Square' version is proven for smooth curves (like those drawn with a pen) but remains one of topology's famous unsolved problems for 'fractal' or extremely jagged curves.
sections.example: A comparison between a smooth 'potato' shape (where a square is easily found) and a snowflake-like fractal coastline where mathematicians are still searching for the definitive proof.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Power of Topology
sections.content: Summarize how looking at a problem from a higher dimension (moving from 2D curves to 3D surfaces like the Möbius strip) can solve puzzles that seem impossible in the original space.
sections.example: The explorer from Section 1 realizes that by looking at the 'map' of all possible pairs, the solution to his tower placement was hidden in the geometry of the paper itself.
